sources.headline: Carney looks to China as Trump tariffs squeeze Canada's car industry
sources.text: Figure caption, Carney eyes 'other options' for embattled Canadian auto sector on China tripByNadine YousifSenior Canada reporterUpdated 4 hours agoCanada's car industry has become one of the clearest stress tests for Ottawa as it grapples with US tariffs on the sector.Now Prime Minister Mark Carney has signalled that he is looking to China, where he is on a visit for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit (Apec), as part of the solution. But that avenue is not without controversy, and is once again drawing the ire of those close to Donald Trump. While in Cambodia earlier this week, Carney told reporters that Canada could turn to European and Asian carmakers to save its auto manufacturing sector if a trade deal with the US could not be reached.If Canadian auto workers are "not fully utilised in a North American context, that provides other opportunities. "Canada's going to move forward either way," he said.He went on to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping in China on Tuesday for their second head-to-head in less than a year. The two talked of the importance of developing their relations, and Carney said they had agreed to further tariff cuts.Neither side mentioned vehicles specifically, though analysts suggest the issue will have been prominent in their minds.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Carney and Xi met on Tuesday to discuss cooperation and trade ahead of this week's Apec summitIn January, Carney said that opening the door to China's electric vehicles, external (EVs) could result in investment into Canadian-owned companies and the creation of manufacturing jobs in the sector. American tariffs on imports of Canadian-made vehicles have led to thousands of job losses in Canada and anxiety over the future, as 90% of cars made in Canada are shipped to and sold in the US.At the same time, China has been eyeing Canada as a potential entry-point to the North American EV market. Earlier this year, Canada announced that it would let in 49,000 EVs from China at a low tariff rate, with plans to raise that quota gradually to 70,000 by 2030.The move was a significant break from the US, which tariffs Chinese EVs heavily to protect domestic manufacturing.Peter Navarro, Trump's senior counsel for trade and manufacturing, warned the prime minister against cosying up to China in a post on X, external."Are u really threatening to play China off the US? This is offensive in the extreme," he wrote on Monday. "You should be far more worried China is going to eat Canada alive."His comments were reposted by Pete Hoekstra, the US ambassador to Canada.Image source, Maninder Sidhu/XImage caption, Canada's international trade minister Maninder Sidhu toured a Chinese EV plant earlier this monthChinese EV manufacturers like BYD and Chery have already been lobbying the Canadian government for market access.Last week, Canada's Minister of International Trade Maninder Sidhu toured a Chery plant in China, external. He told reporters afterwards that Canadians could expect to see affordable Chinese EVs in Canada by early 2027.These moves come as the toll of US tariffs on Canada's auto sector has become harder to ignore.Stellantis, a multinational car manufacturer that made models like the Dodge Challenger in Canada, recently announced it would sell its assembly plant in Brampton, Ontario.The facility had been idle since 2023 for a planned retooling, but what was supposed to be a temporary shutdown became permanent after Trump's tariffs.The sale has led to speculation that a Chinese EV manufacturer could move into the facility, after Canadian media outlet CTV News reported, external, citing anonymous sources, that Stellantis was planning to lease back 25% of its plant to assemble "affordable" EVs.The idea is unpopular with Ontario Premier Doug Ford. In a letter to Carney, he warned against opening the door for Chinese EV kits to be assembled at the Brampton plant. China overwhelmingly builds its cars at home and ships them whole - or to be assembled in kits - overseas.Lynette Ong, director of the China Governance Lab at the University of Toronto, said introducing Chinese auto manufacturing in Canada would be "controversial" due to fears that Canadian jobs could be lost and that the North American industry could be eroded."We want to make sure they're hiring Canadian workers, that they are helping train Canadian workers and that they are transferring the technology over," Ong said.Carney noted there are "clear guardrails" in how Canada deals with China, including barring work on sensitive matters like artificial intelligence and critical minerals.Canada has also eyed other partnerships. It is notably pursuing associate member status with the EU, and had signed a free trade deal with the Philippines earlier this week. Just how much Canada is willing to embrace Chinese manufacturing, however, still depends on the outcome of ongoing US-Canada trade talks.Progress has been made in negotiations, Carney recently said, but differences remain. It is unclear if Trump and Carney will speak on the sidelines of the Apec summit later this week.Figure caption, Why China is winning the global EV race

sources.headline: China, Canada expand tariff relief after Carney-Xi meeting
sources.text: China offers tariff cuts on Canadian pork and seafood, as Canada extends exemptions for Chinese steel and aluminium.Canada and China have agreed to cut tariffs on more goods, as Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney continues to look to decrease his country’s dependence on the United States amid President Donald Trump’s tariffs.Meeting on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen on Tuesday, Carney and Chinese President Xi Jinping announced new tariff remissions, building on an agreement they made in January to open up trade and start to repair a strained diplomatic relationship.Recommended Stories list of 4 itemslist 1 of 4Trump, Xi and Putin to hold first three-way summit in Chinalist 2 of 4Southeast Asian leaders to meet as Trump visit highlights trade disruptionlist 3 of 4Trump-Xi-Putin trilateral meeting at APEC: What to expectlist 4 of 4ASEAN summit: Who’s attending and what’s at stake?end of listChina will offer tariff relief on about 400 million Canadian dollars ($280m) worth of Canadian exports, including frozen pork and seafood, said a statement from Carney’s office.Canada, in exchange, will keep tariff exemptions for certain Chinese steel and aluminium products in place for another two years, and add remissions to another 32 steel and aluminium items that Canada doesn’t have enough of.Xi said stronger ties served both countries’ interests and supported global stability and prosperity.“This is the right choice,” he said.Carney praised the greater predictability in the relationship and said Canada was ahead of schedule on its goal of increasing exports to China by 50 percent by the end of the decade.Under the January agreement, Canada lowered its 100 percent tariff on Chinese electric vehicles to 6.1 percent, allowing an initial 49,000 vehicles into the country each year. That cap is set to rise to 70,000 over five years.In return, China agreed to lower tariffs on Canadian agricultural products and recently extended relief for canola meal, peas, lobster and crab for another two years.The deal comes a day after Carney said Canada could turn to Chinese automakers if talks with Washington fail to hold together the closely integrated North American auto industry.“We have the best auto workers in the world, and we want them fully deployed, full opportunity, in an integrated North American market,” Carney told reporters in Cambodia on Monday. “That market has become less integrated because of US trade actions.”The comments prompted a backlash from White House trade adviser Peter Navarro, who responded by asking whether Carney was threatening to “play China off the US”.“This is offensive in the extreme,” he said, adding that Carney should be more worried that China would “eat Canada alive”.Carney has made looking to markets beyond the US a central part of his economic strategy, as Trump’s tariffs hit Canadian industries, including auto manufacturing, as well as steel and aluminium.Trade talks between Ottawa and Washington broke down in August, but Carney said on Saturday that he’d spoken with Trump and senior officials, and that while differences remained, there was progress towards a possible deal.He also met with Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum on Tuesday, with both countries reaffirming their commitment to renew the Canada-United States-Mexico Agreement, according to Carney’s office.One year after Carney visited Mexico, during which they launched a strategic partnership, the two leaders agreed to keep expanding bilateral trade and investment. They also highlighted a 19-percent increase in merchandise trade in the first nine months of this year, compared with the same period last year.

sources.headline: Canada could work with Chinese automakers if US trade talks fail, says Carney
sources.text: The prime minister of Canada, Mark Carney, said the country could turn to Chinese automakers if trade negotiations with the US president, Donald Trump, failed to preserve an integrated North American auto industry.Carney’s comments in Cambodia on Monday came ahead of a planned meeting with Chinese leader Xi Jinping this week in Shenzhen, China, where auto manufacturing is expected to be discussed. The two leaders reached an agreement in January allowing tens of thousands of Chinese electric vehicles into Canada at reduced tariffs.“We have the best auto workers in the world, and we want them fully deployed, full opportunity, in an integrated North American market,” Carney told reporters in Cambodia. “That market has become less integrated because of US trade actions.”He said on Monday that negotiations with the US remained his priority, but their outcome could determine whether Canada pursues alternatives involving European, Chinese or Japanese automakers. A day earlier in Manila, in the Philippines, Carney said any trade agreement with Washington must leave Canada with a viable auto industry.Asked whether potential Chinese investment was leverage in US negotiations, Carney replied: “It’s not leverage. But action, reaction.“If they [Canada’s auto workers] are not fully utilized in a North American context, that provides other opportunities,” Carney said. “Canada is going to move forward either way.”The Detroit Three – Ford, General Motors and Stellantis – operate factories across Canada, the US and Mexico, with parts sometimes crossing borders multiple times before a vehicle is completed. Trump has repeatedly pushed automakers to move production to the US from Canada.Carney said any Chinese investment would have to involve substantial manufacturing in Canada rather than simply assembling imported parts. He said it would need proper labor standards, manufacturing facilities and domestic supply chains that expand over time, including Canadian critical minerals used in electric vehicles.“It’s not just about kit cars,” he said. “There has to be a manufacturing aspect involved.”Under a January agreement, Canada reduced its 100% tariff on Chinese electric vehicles to 6.1%, initially allowing up to 49,000 vehicles annually, with the cap increasing over time. In exchange, China agreed to lower tariffs on Canadian agricultural products, including canola.Carney said at the time that he expected the agreement to attract Chinese investment in Canada’s auto industry and create jobs.The deal drew criticism from Ontario premier Doug Ford, whose province is the center of Canada’s auto industry. Ford warned that allowing Chinese electric vehicles into Canada could threaten Canadian jobs and jeopardize access to the US market.Trump’s tariffs have disrupted Canada’s auto industry, which relies heavily on cross-border production. Canada recently threatened to sue Stellantis after the automaker shifted planned Jeep Compass production from Brampton, Ontario, to Illinois and agreed to sell its idled Canadian assembly plant.Carney said Saturday that he had spoken at length with Trump and senior US officials and that the two countries were making progress toward a possible trade agreement, although differences remained.

sources.headline: Carney to meet Xi on Tuesday to talk food, energy and financial services
sources.text: OTTAWA, Nov 16 - Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney will meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping on Tuesday ahead of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) meeting, seeking to deepen ties on food, energy and financial services.Carney in January became the first Canadian prime minister to visit China in nearly a decade, a major plank of his strategy to reduce Canada's overwhelming economic reliance on the United States. Tuesday's meeting in Shenzhen, a southern Chinese tech and manufacturing hub, will be the third time Carney has met Xi since becoming prime minister; he also met Xi on the sidelines of last year's APEC meeting in South Korea.Carney is participating in various Asian summits to continue his work of trade and diplomatic diversification. He said on Sunday his discussion with Xi would also include the evolution of China's role in the international system."This is part of a process that began when I came into government, of normalization of the economic relationship between Canada and China," Carney said from Cambodia, alluding to the fractious relationship between the two countries under previous Prime Minister Justin Trudeau.Chinese automakers BYD, Geely and Chery have taken steps to enter the Canadian market since Canada approved imports of 49,000 cars annually at a low tariff rate of 6.1%. The quota is set to rise to 70,000 cars over five years.Carney said trade actions taken by the US have complicated the previously integrated North American autos market and that there are ongoing discussions with Trump and his administration to try to resolve those issues."Depending on where that settles, there'll be other options: European options, Asian options of course, Chinese (and) Japanese," Carney said.US President Donald Trump has threatened to raise tariffs on Canadian cars, trucks and auto parts to 50% from 25% on January 1.PROTECTING CANADA'S SECURITYCritics have warned Canada's closer ties to China could jeopardize Canadian security. Human rights groups have also decried Carney's willingness to do more business with Beijing after China jailed pro-democracy media mogul Jimmy Lai and secretly executed four Canadians in China last year, and after Canada found evidence China interfered in at least two federal elections. China has said it had no interest in interfering with Canada's internal affairs."Carney has done the difficult part of stabilizing the relationship with China, but now he's entering an even more challenging phase of actually balancing selective economic engagement with protecting Canada's economic and national security," said Vina Nadjibulla, co-founder of the Centre for Strategic Statecraft think tank. "We need to have some clarity on how Canada will be managing these sensitivities and it's unclear if that level of detail has yet been communicated to China."Carney has repeatedly said that engaging China does not mean endorsement and says Canada must have a relationship with countries where it hopes to effect change.China also lowered tariffs on Canadian canola seed after Carney's January visit, and recently extended tariff relief for canola meal, lobsters, crabs and peas for two more years.Canada has exported 2.8 million metric tons of canola seed to China so far this year. Prior to Carney's visit, new sales to China ended when duties were imposed in August 2025. Canadian farmers hope to see China reduce a 25% tariff on Canadian pork and related products.Shipments of Canadian crude oil to China have increased about 37% in 2026, according to a Reuters calculation based on LSEG data.Carney landed in Shenzhen on Monday and is scheduled to meet with Xi at 10:30 a.m. Tuesday (0230 GMT). REUTERS

China dismisses Canada’s interference concerns ahead of leaders’ meeting

Beijing pushes back after Mark Carney pledges to raise the issue during talks with President Xi Jinping

Agence France-Presse
Published: 3:48am, 11 Nov 2026Updated: 4:46pm, 11 Nov 2026

China dismissed concerns on Wednesday that it interferes in Canadian affairs, after Prime Minister Mark Carney said he would raise the issue with President Xi Jinping when the two meet at a summit next week.

A Canadian public inquiry last year into allegations of election meddling identified China as “the most active perpetrator of foreign interference targeting Canada’s democratic institutions”.

Carney said on Tuesday that he would discuss “many things” with Xi during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit in Shenzhen, including efforts to broaden bilateral trade and the importance of “non-interference in our affairs by China”.

Beijing has consistently denied allegations that it interferes in the internal affairs of other states.

“China always sticks to the principle of non-interference in other countries’ internal affairs … and has never had any interest in interfering in Canada’s internal affairs,” foreign ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun told a news conference on Wednesday.

The final report of Canada’s public inquiry into foreign interference, however, concluded that China “views Canada as a high-priority target” and meddled in the 2019 and 2021 federal elections.

Federal police have also investigated reports that Beijing operates illegal police stations on Canadian soil tasked with harassing or intimidating Chinese expatriates.

Carney visited China in January as part of his push to restore ties that crumbled under former prime minister Justin Trudeau.

Carney has said Canada needs to urgently diversify its foreign trade to reduce dependence on the United States, and has made China and India key targets.
